blogs.title: Platform engineering needs to become more human…and less
blogs.content: Posted on November 11, 2026 by Alejandro Chirinos, Control Plane CNCF projects highlighted in this post Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job. If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane. Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson. Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand. And even though I was pretty consistent and logical, and so were (most of) my engineering colleagues, things could get messy fast. That’s where platform engineering came in, and that’s when I met Dan. Dan Wilson was this brilliant platform engineer at SAP/Concur. He was one of the early open source contributors to a lot of fundamental projects. He knew Kubernetes like an old friend, and he could make your cloud infrastructure sing. I loved working with Dan because he got my logically organized code to production more logically and a heckuva lot faster. A merge to main kicked off a containerized build, then unit tests, integration tests, and a security scan, and every stage had to pass before the image was promoted to the next environment. Deployments were declarative, the desired state lived in version control, and Kubernetes made the cluster match it. It warmed my engineer’s heart to watch the CI/CD pipelines hum through their stage gates. But the whole process, the whole platform, was still made for engineers. It assumed deep technical knowledge. It required strict compliance with established protocols. It wasn’t hard. It was just logical. Just a little robotic, but that was fine because it was designed for people who were a little robotic…at least a little more robotic than the average person. I mean, what engineer would try to name a production database final_v2_USE_THIS_ONE? (Several, it turns out. But they had the decency to feel bad about it.) The platform never had to defend against this behavior, because the people using it were not completely normal humans. We designed internal platforms for engineers who read the docs (allegedly), knew what a rollback was, and had a decent sense of when not to deploy. That is so Oct 2025 But then Opus 4.5 was released and everything changed. Or more specifically, every one changed. Everyone changed from being a normal human to being an engineer…just without the pocket protectors, inside jokes, and strict adherence to protocol. The systems that took me weekends at Disney could now be vibe-coded by the receptionist in a few hours. And they would work (they might not be secure or performant, and they might be a usability train wreck, but bear with me). Everyone was now an engineer because everyone now had agents. They had their own little fleet of Dorons doing their bidding. GitHub’s 2025 Octoverse report counted more than 36 million new developers joining in a single year, more than one every second, for a total past 180 million. What this means for platform engineering is that now the humans using the platform act more like humans than they ever have. They improvise. If the form won’t take their input, they find another way in. They share the password because sharing is polite . They ask the person at the next desk instead of reading the docs, and they copy whatever worked last time, even if last time was a different project in a different region. They name things for other humans, so production ends up running something called “Q4 launch page FINAL (Jen’s edits).” These aren’t really flaws. In most of the company, they’re called “initiative”. Or “creativity”. But you might also call it “chaos”. Of course, engineers are creative too. But what we’re about to see…what we’re already seeing…is an EXPLOSION in creativity entering the software development world. Because now creativity of all sorts, from all sorts of very non-robotic people, has been given direct access to the code. Musicians. Copywriters. Recruiters. The finance lead who has opinions about dashboards. These are people who were never going to learn a programming language, and now they don’t have to. They bring taste, empathy, and a feel for what customers want, which the old pipeline often filtered out long before anything reached production. They also bring their own idea of what “done” means and no idea how a typical internal developer platform operates. But these new humans and this explosion in creativity are here. And they’re not going away. So platform engineering has to find a way to harness all this creativity without it taking anything important offline or leaking company secrets all over the internet. Making room for the more-human builders Here’s what I think needs to happen for that to take place. The rules have to move out of people’s heads and into the platform. For as long as most of us have done this work, the guardrails lived inside the engineers…at least in large part. Nobody had to tell a senior engineer not to expose a database to the internet, not to paste an API key into a chat window, or not to name a production table test . They had learned it the hard way, usually at 2am, usually once. Those lessons got passed along in code reviews, in onboarding, in the raised eyebrow of a colleague. The platform didn’t have to enforce what its users already believed. It could be a little naive, because its users weren’t. That arrangement is finished. The copywriter shipping a landing page has never been paged at 2am, and I hope she never is. The recruiter building an interview scheduler doesn’t know a public bucket from a private one, and there’s no reason she should. The finance lead with opinions about dashboards will happily connect one to the production database, because that’s where the real numbers are. They’re doing what every smart, motivated person does with a new tool: click around until something lights up. So the platform has to know these things on their behalf. Every app has to get its own identity the moment it’s created, scoped to what it needs and nothing more. Secrets must get injected at runtime, not handed to a person, so there’s nothing to paste into Slack and nothing to save in a notes app for later. Policies have to check every change before it lands: no public endpoints without a reason, no direct line from a dashboard to the production database, no resources without an owner. Every deployment has to go out small, get watched, and roll itself back if the numbers turn bad. When the platform does have to say no, it should say it the way a good colleague would. Not “Denied by policy 0042.” More like, “This would make your customer list public on the internet. Here’s the setting that keeps it internal.” An error message is the closest thing these builders will ever get to that raised eyebrow, so write it like one. Done well, most of these new more-human builders never notice any of this. And that’s as it should be. Agents, the less-human builders But wait a minute. We’ve had an explosion in human creativity entering the platform engineering chat, but we’ve also had a super explosion in agents…who are more robotic than any of (well, most of) the engineers I’ve ever worked with. Here’s what I mean. An agent will read every line of your documentation, which already puts it ahead of most of us. It follows instructions exactly. It doesn’t ge...

blogs.title: CloudNativePG becomes a CNCF Incubating Project
blogs.content: Posted on November 10, 2026 by CloudNativePG Maintainers CNCF projects highlighted in this post The CNCF Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) voted to accept CloudNativePG as a CNCF incubating project . CloudNativePG is an open source Kubernetes operator that manages the full lifecycle of highly available PostgreSQL clusters. Organizations across financial services, insurance, telecommunications, automotive, retail, and the public sector use it to run production PostgreSQL in Kubernetes without bolting on separate failover tooling. “What started as a crazy idea of our small team in Prato, Italy, in 2019 is becoming a standard way of running PostgreSQL in production, with the declarative configuration, standardisation, immutability, and security that Kubernetes brings,” said Gabriele Bartolini, VP and Distinguished Engineer at EDB, co-founder and maintainer of CloudNativePG. “We did not accept the status quo: we decided to push both PostgreSQL and Kubernetes into new territory. It is challenging, and there have been tough moments, but today we have one of the best ways to run PostgreSQL at large scale. Incubation is another rung on the ladder, and the journey continues.” CloudNativePG’s Milestones and Ecosystem Development CloudNativePG uses a primary/standby architecture with native streaming replication. Instead of relying on external tools, it integrates directly with the Kubernetes API, so the cluster’s state is declared, reconciled, and observed the same way as any other Kubernetes resource. The operator handles automated failover, rolling updates, self-healing, connection pooling, continuous backup, and point-in-time recovery. It runs the PostgreSQL instances as pods it manages directly, without StatefulSets. EDB, a leading contributor to PostgreSQL for over two decades, created CloudNativePG and submitted it to the CNCF in 2024, before it was officially accepted as a sandbox project on January 21, 2025. Since then, the community has shipped five releases (1.26 through 1.30), plus ongoing patch releases. The latest, v1.30.1, was published on September 23, 2026. Highlights include: Declarative, offline in-place major version upgrades (1.26) Dynamic loading of PostgreSQL extensions (1.27) Quorum-based failover promoted to stable (1.28) Dynamic network access control (1.29) A Lease-based mechanism for safe primary election and a new DatabaseRole resource with automatically issued and renewed TLS client certificates for password-free authentication (1.30) The project also participates in the CNCF LFX Mentorship program and formalized its governance in a dedicated governance repository, with public, transparent votes recorded as GitHub issues. CloudNativePG connects to the broader cloud native ecosystem with documented integrations including External Secrets and Cilium . It also works with cert-manager for TLS certificates, exposes metrics through a built-in Prometheus exporter, and offers a Keycloak OAuth validator . A September 2026 CNCF blog shows this in practice with OpenBao running on Kubernetes with CloudNativePG as its storage backend. The setup uses a three-instance cluster with quorum-based synchronous replication to protect data during failover. DatabaseRole resources issue and renew TLS client certificates, so no database role needs a password. Explicit pg_hba rules require certificate authentication, and scheduling rules keep PostgreSQL on dedicated nodes in separate zones. More than 50 organizations are listed as production adopters , including IBM, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, GEICO Tech, Akamai, Novo Nordisk, REWE International, PZU Group, Tesla, Ericsson, and the Dutch Tax and Customs Administration (Belastingdienst). Ten of those were added in 2026 alone. CloudNativePG’s Roadmap The CloudNativePG roadmap includes release v1.31, planned for around December 2026, and v1.32 for around March 2027. Version 1.31 ships with native Barman Cloud support, which moves fully to the CNPG-I plugin architecture starting with v1.32. Klio, a multi-tiered cloud native backup and recovery solution built on CNPG-I, launches before the end of 2026. Beyond releases, the project plans to: Raise its compliance with the Open Source Project Security Baseline (OSPS Baseline) to level 3 Apply for CNCF Graduation in 2027 Publish blueprints that integrate PostgreSQL with other CNCF projects through CloudNativePG, such as OpenTelemetry, Keycloak and SPIFFE/SPIRE Publish a set of distributable tests that anyone can run to validate an environment, followed by an official CloudNativePG conformance program, to enable more supported distributions and third-party plugins built on CNPG-I Resume participation in the CNCF LFX Mentorship program Main Components CloudNativePG’s main components consist of the following: Operator and Cluster resource: the controller and central custom resource that declare and reconcile an entire PostgreSQL cluster. It manages Pods, volumes, Services, and Secrets directly, without StatefulSets, orchestrating failover and rolling updates instance by instance. Instance Manager: runs as PID 1 in the PostgreSQL container, with no sidecars. It manages the PostgreSQL lifecycle and promotion, reports health and replication lag, serves database-aware probes, and reconciles Database, Publication, Subscription, and DatabaseRole resources inside PostgreSQL. Operand images and image catalogs: maintained PostgreSQL container images, with declarative catalogs for managing versions across clusters. CNPG-I: the plugin interface that lets the community extend CloudNativePG without forking it, which is where backup and recovery solutions plug in. Backup and recovery: the Barman Cloud plugin today, and Klio, a multi-tiered cloud native backup and recovery solution built on CNPG-I and launching soon. Tooling: the kubectl cnpg plugin, Helm charts, dashboards, and PgBouncer-based connection pooling. Notable Milestones 9,500 GitHub Stars 7,301 pull requests 3,905 issues 4,403 Contributors from 1487 organizations and 49 countries 274M Operator downloads 192M Postgres operand downloads CNCF-Hosted Projects The CNCF TOC provides technical leadership to the cloud native projects and community. It defines and maintains the foundation’s technical vision, approves new projects, and stewards them across maturity levels. The TOC also aligns projects within the overall ecosystem , sets cross-cutting standards and best practices, and works with end users to ensure long-term sustainability. As part of its principles , the TOC evaluates and supports projects as they meet requirements for incubation and continue progressing toward graduation. As a CNCF-hosted project, CloudNativePG is part of a neutral foundation aligned with its technical interests, as well as the larger Linux Foundation, which provides governance, marketing support, and community outreach. CloudNativePG joins incubating technologies Artifact Hub, Backstage, Chaos Mesh, Cloud Custodian, Confidential Containers, Container Network Interface (CNI), Contour, Cortex, Emissary-ingress, Fluid, gRPC, HAMi, k8gb, Keycloak, KServe, Kubescape, KubeVela, KubeVirt, Lima, Litmus, Longhorn, Meshery, metal3-io, Microcks, NATS, Notary Project, OpenCost, OpenFeature, OpenFGA, OpenKruise, OpenYurt, Operator Framework, Strimzi, Tekton, Thanos, Volcano, and wasmCloud. For detailed maturity requirements at each level, please visit the CNCF Graduation Criteria . Share

blogs.title: Welcoming OpenShell to the CNCF: Open Governance to Secure Agentic AI
blogs.content: Posted on November 10, 2026 by Jonathan Bryce (CNCF), Ali Golshan (NVIDIA) CNCF projects highlighted in this post Today at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) welcomes OpenShell as a Sandbox project. NVIDIA has contributed OpenShell, an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous AI agents, to the foundation’s community-led home. As organizations put AI agents to work, they need to give agents real capability without giving them unchecked access to data, secrets, or networks. This requires enforcement outside of the agents, right within the infrastructure that the agents run on. OpenShell does exactly that: it manages and monitors agent behavior, provides and enforces policy-based boundaries for what it can do. OpenShell is adopting Cedar, another CNCF project, as its policy language. It’s a great example of CNCF projects building on one another. Why this belongs in the cloud native community Agents are becoming part of cloud native infrastructure, and the layer that governs them should be shared, vendor-neutral, and open to everyone who depends on it. OpenShell already reflects that spirit. Core contributors from NVIDIA, Red Hat, Docker, and Canonical have worked on the project since its inception. Their early involvement, alongside many additional organizations adopting OpenShell shows broad industry agreement on the need for dependable controls for agentic systems. “Open source is the foundation of enterprise trust. As agents become part of cloud native infrastructure, the controls around them need to be open, auditable, and built together with the ecosystem. Bringing OpenShell to the CNCF puts governance of the project in the hands of the community. Red Hat has always believed that innovation thrives where collaboration is open, and we’re excited to help steward OpenShell alongside NVIDIA and the broader ecosystem.” — Chris Wright, Chief Technology Officer and Senior Vice President of Global Engineering, Red Hat Contributing OpenShell to the CNCF as a neutral foundation is a natural next step to expand and grow the OpenShell project. It has adopted the CNCF Code of Conduct, runs a public RFC process, and follows a governance model with explicit vendor-neutrality commitments. By contributing OpenShell alongside partners and maintainers from across the industry, NVIDIA aims to make secure AI available to all, under the same open governance model that supports other CNCF projects. Built for an ecosystem No two organizations run agents the same way. They use different infrastructure, secret stores, inference providers, and governance practices, and those choices change over time. OpenShell is designed to fit this variety through well-defined extension points for providers, compute, governance and approval workflows, policy enforcement, isolation, and credential management. Teams can adopt it incrementally and swap in what they already run. It also gives vendors, integrators, and end users clear places to contribute. What changes, and what doesn’t OpenShell is moving from NVIDIA’s GitHub repository to a neutral organization, ai-openshell. Working groups and special interest groups will form around integrated components and cross-cutting topics such as observability. The core engineering efforts from NVIDIA will continue, while we welcome contributions from other interested parties. Ways to participate Whether your organization already uses OpenShell or is just exploring it, contributing is the best way to shape its future. Areas where help is especially welcome include: Extension implementations. Reference implementations for compute, credential management, inference, and logging, along with shared documentation and conformance tests so third-party integrations behave consistently.
